# Hedge Fund Accounting

For hedge fund CFOs, controllers and fund administrators.

## Accounting Capabilities

- Share classes hold the terms for unitized funds. Fee classes group investors in capital-based funds. The Share Classes and Fee Terms screens record these arrangements for funds whose investors have different fee terms.

- Fee Terms records management fee rates, calculation basis and step-down bands. The Fees screen holds period offset sources. The fee configuration supplies the terms used when the period management fee is calculated.

- The Fees screen calculates period management fees from the fund's saved terms. Accruals can be posted and reversed, giving the period fee a corresponding accounting entry in the fund's books.

- NAV records preliminary, final and restated fund values, including share-class lines. The NAV and period-close screens show the fund's strike workflow, with class results available through the share register.

- Capital Accounts shows investor balances for the selected fund. Accounting checks compare investor capital snapshots with general ledger capital, giving the investor balances a defined tie to the fund's capital accounts.

- Investor statements show opening capital, contributions, distributions, allocated income and expenses, fees and ending capital. The statement draws these amounts from the investor's recorded account and the fund's reporting period.

- Reporting groups investor statement production into runs. The team generates, reviews and publishes the statements, with failures recorded per account so an individual statement failure is isolated within the run.

- NAV supports share-class and series values, with final period strikes and daily estimates. Daily NAV estimates retain their grade and are superseded by the period close, preserving the distinction between daily and closed values.

## Related Notes

- [Equalization and the mid-period subscriber](https://1494labs.com/notes/equalization-and-the-mid-period-subscriber/)

- [High-water marks and partial redemptions](https://1494labs.com/notes/high-water-marks-and-partial-redemptions/)

- [Side pockets and investor participation](https://1494labs.com/notes/side-pockets-and-investor-participation/)

## Questions

### Can investors in one fund have different fee terms?

Yes. Unitized funds use share classes, and capital-based funds use fee classes. The Share Classes and Fee Terms screens record these groups and their terms within the fund.

### Can a calculated management fee post to the books?

Yes. After fee terms are configured, Fees calculates the period accrual and provides posting and reversal actions. The posted accrual records the management fee in the fund's accounting books.

### Can I keep daily NAV estimates and final class NAV?

Yes. NAV supports daily estimates and final period strikes with share-class and series values. Daily estimates carry an estimate grade and are superseded by the close when final NAV is struck.

### Do investor capital accounts tie to general ledger capital?

Yes. The accounting checks compare investor capital balances with the fund's general ledger capital. Capital Accounts displays the investor balances. The tie is an accounting invariant checked across the book.

### Can I review investor statements before publishing a run?

Yes. Statement runs group generation, review and publication. Each account has its own result, allowing the team to inspect a failed item and review the generated statements before publishing the run.

A period an investor was not in is marked as a gap.

**Six managers, each at cost and at value.** The date each was last revalued sits on the row, because the age of an input is part of the number.

![A cash movements blotter of settled movements: investments into underlying managers, investor subscriptions, and transfers between the fund's own cash accounts, each with its source and counterparty.](https://1494labs.com/assets/screens/cash-movements.61bcbb09.jpg)

**Every movement carries its source, counterparty and settlement status.** Payments to underlying managers name the manager, subscriptions name the investor, and a transfer between the fund's own accounts is derived from the journal entry that moved it. One cash sub-ledger, reconciled against the bank statement.

![Seven series of one share class, one per subscription month from January 2024 to February 2026, each issued at 100.00 in its own inception period, with the January 2024 series marked as the lead.](https://1494labs.com/assets/screens/series.7f98fbc2.jpg)

**One series per subscription month.** Each is issued at 100.00 in its own inception period and measured against its own high-water mark.

![Four scheduled incentive crystallizations, two at December 2024 and two at December 2025, each posted with the amount crystallized.](https://1494labs.com/assets/screens/crystallizations.da9bddb9.jpg)

**Crystallized per series, each December.** After a down 2025, the 2024 series stayed below their high-water marks and paid nothing; the series opened at the lows paid.

# Holding Company and Family Office Entity Accounting

For family office finance teams accounting for holding companies, partnerships and trusts.

## Accounting Capabilities

- Fund setup records the legal entity, base currency and fiscal year. Closed-end funds also carry vintage, fund term, extension dates and hard cap, so the fund record contains the terms used by the accounting team.

- Allocations distributes income, expenses and gains through recorded ownership. The allocation screen includes a cascade preview and confirmation for structures with multiple ownership layers, connecting fund results with the investors above them.

- Reporting provides the trial balance for the fund, including the balance frozen at close and its revisions. The frozen balance preserves the ledger totals used for that close and subsequent review.

- Fund Statements provides an income statement, balance sheet, statement of changes in net assets and cash-flow statement for one fund and period. The reporting screen uses the selected fund and reporting period.

- Family Office shows holding companies, family partnerships, trusts, personal accounts and individuals in a household structure. Fund setup records vehicle types, including GRATs, and the structure chart displays the ownership layers.

- Trust beneficiary interests are recorded against the trust. The Family Office Net Worth view displays the beneficiary information beside the trust, keeping the beneficiary interest on the recorded trust vehicle.

- The household structure chart traces ownership through entities. Ownership weights come from the capital holdings, and Allocations uses those relationships to carry income through the chain, including structures with shared ownership subtrees.

- Family vehicles can hold private fund interests, portfolio companies and internal fund interests. Underlying Funds and Companies record the private investments, with fund capital activity attached to the holding vehicle's investment record.

- The Family Office Net Worth view groups household value by category, holder and period. It includes movement between periods and supports the household reporting package, giving family finance teams a consolidated value view.

- Family Office includes household performance, principal cash flows, exposure, concentration and book-to-market reconciliation. These views sit with the household records so the team can review value, cash movement and investment exposure for the family.

## Terms

Holdco means holding company. Family partnerships, trusts, GRATs and personal accounts are vehicle types in the household structure. Ownership follows the recorded capital holdings.

## Questions

### Can I represent a household's companies, partnerships and trusts?

Yes. Vehicle setup and the household structure chart support holding companies, partnerships, trusts, personal accounts and individuals. GRAT is a recorded vehicle type. The chart shows the layers represented in the household book.

### Can I display beneficiary interests alongside a trust?

Yes. Beneficiary interests can be recorded against a trust, and the Family Office Net Worth view displays the beneficiary information. The interests are memo records on that trust.

### Can income allocations follow ownership across family entities?

Yes. The structure chart and Allocations use ownership weights derived from capital holdings. Income cascades follow those relationships across the household's entities, including shared ownership subtrees.

### Can I see household net worth by entity and asset category?

Yes. Family Office provides consolidated net worth by category, holder and period, including movement. Household reporting packages can include the net worth results for the family's reporting process.

### Can I prepare the financial statements for one fund and period?

Yes. Fund Statements includes the income statement, balance sheet, statement of changes in net assets and cash-flow statement. These reports use one fund and reporting period for the financial statement set.

## Follow one month from income to investor capital.

One month of a reference fund, in two steps: what the fund earned after
its management fee, then where it ended up in six investors' capital accounts.

| Net income for the month | $145,284.59 |
| --- | --- |
| Management fee, through the fee calculation | −$19,314.66 |
| Net profit and loss to allocate | $125,969.93 |

| Opening investor capital | $23,499,503.07 |
| --- | --- |
| Net profit and loss allocated | +$125,969.93 |
| Ending investor capital, and the NAV | $23,625,473.00 |

| Investor account | Opening | Net P&L | Ending |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| WBE-001-A | $6,284,337.90 | $33,687.42 | $6,318,025.32 |
| WBE-003-A | $5,459,391.06 | $29,265.26 | $5,488,656.32 |
| WBE-006-A | $3,774,244.32 | $20,231.97 | $3,794,476.29 |
| WBE-002-A | $3,420,147.35 | $18,333.82 | $3,438,481.17 |
| WBE-005-A | $2,519,062.68 | $13,503.53 | $2,532,566.21 |
| WBE-004-A | $2,042,319.76 | $10,947.93 | $2,053,267.69 |
| Six accounts | $23,499,503.07 | $125,969.93 | $23,625,473.00 |

**Six investor accounts reconcile to the fund's ending NAV of $23,625,473.00.** Management fees and expenses are attributed to the accounts that bear them, so a fee that reaches NAV reaches the capital account it belongs to.

# Liquidity Forecasting and Commitment Pacing

For allocators and fund managers planning commitments, deployment and cash flows.

## Commitments and Recorded Cash Flows

- Capital Accounts shows unfunded commitments by investor and fund. A fund setting chooses the historical or spot measure, so the reported unfunded amount follows the accounting basis selected for that fund.

- Fund Statements provides an income statement, balance sheet, statement of changes in net assets and cash-flow statement for one fund and period. The reporting screen uses the selected fund and reporting period.

- Investor statements show opening capital, contributions, distributions, allocated income and expenses, fees and ending capital. The statement draws these amounts from the investor's recorded account and the fund's reporting period.

- Underlying fund positions carry manager-reported marks and performance. Valuations and Look-through show position IRR, TVPI, DPI and RVPI, with support for late manager statements and the resulting restatement of reported values.

## Terms

Commitment pacing uses a commitment budget across vintages. Unfunded commitments, expected calls, distributions recycled and available cash describe the funding plan. The accounting coverage listed here supplies unfunded balances and recorded fund reporting.

## Questions

### Can I see unfunded commitments by investor?

Yes. Capital Accounts reports unfunded commitments per investor and per fund. The fund's setting selects the historical or spot measure used in that view, giving the team a defined basis for the outstanding amount.

### Can I record late manager marks and underlying-fund performance?

Yes. Underlying fund positions retain manager marks and position performance, including IRR, TVPI, DPI and RVPI. The valuation process supports late quarter statements and restatement of the affected reported values.

### Can I prepare the financial statements for one fund and period?

Yes. Fund Statements includes the income statement, balance sheet, statement of changes in net assets and cash-flow statement. These reports use one fund and reporting period for the financial statement set.

### Can an investor statement show flows, fees and ending capital?

Yes. The capital account statement includes opening capital, contributions, distributions, allocated income and expense, fees and ending capital. It records the period's movement for the investor account and its closing balance.

# A wrong number that agrees with itself

Cash reconciles against the custodian, positions against the administrator.
Both work by comparison, so both are quiet when a figure is wrong and
nothing else in the system holds a second copy of it to disagree.

Controls · roughly 6 minutes

## Where comparison controls stop

Most controls in fund accounting are comparisons: cash against the
custodian, positions against the administrator, the general ledger against
the sub-ledger. They find a great deal. All of them work the same way,
which is that they fire when two records of the same thing differ.

A management fee charged on the wrong base has no second record. Nor does
an allocation that split a period's profit on a stale ownership percentage,
or a high-water mark that was never reduced when an investor redeemed half
their holding. In each case the books balance, every statement foots, and
the investor's capital account is internally consistent. The money was either never charged or charged to the wrong person.

Why this class survives

An audit tests whether the books are consistent, and they are. These
errors tend to surface years later, when somebody rebuilds a fee from
first principles and finds it does not come out where it was booked.

## Doing the arithmetic a second time

A figure with no counterparty to check against has to be checked against
itself: derived again by a different route, from different inputs, and
compared. We do that to every fund on the platform each morning, before
anyone signs in.

Some of what is recomputed:

- ✓**Every capital account rolls forward.**
Opening, plus contributions and withdrawals, plus that account's share of
profit and loss, equals closing, to the penny, with no tolerance, for every account in every period.

- ✓**Ownership sums to one hundred percent**
exactly, with the rounding residual placed deliberately.

- ✓**The fees charged to investors add up to the fee the fund paid**,
side letters and differing rates included. If the parts do not sum to the
pool, one of the two figures is wrong.

- ✓**Every journal entry balances and the trial balance foots**,
checked daily.

- ✓**What a position is carried at agrees with the ledger's carrying value**
through every subscription, redemption and return of capital, so the two
cannot drift apart between valuations.

A failure opens an exception on the same worklist as a cash exception, carrying the
fund, the period, and the two figures that should have agreed.

## Every morning

An error found during the close is found under deadline, by the person with
least appetite for it, when the remaining options are poor. The same error
found on a Tuesday is an afternoon's work, which is most of the argument for running the checks daily.

They also do not sample. Every fund is recomputed every day, including the
ones with no activity, because an absence of activity is itself worth
testing: a fund that has quietly stopped receiving data looks the same as a
fund having a slow month until the quarter closes.

## Knowing whether a check actually ran

A check that never ran reports nothing. A check that ran and passed also
reports nothing. On a dashboard the two are indistinguishable, and the more
conditional a check is, the more often it is the first one.

A rule that applies only to funds with an incentive fee has nothing to
examine in a book that has none. It stays quiet, and so does a rule that ran
and found nothing wrong.

The distinction

A check that has never had anything to examine has not passed. Counting
it alongside the ones that did overstates what the system has actually
demonstrated.

So the morning run reports what was never exercised as well as what failed,
naming each check that no fund gave it anything to work on. Some of that is
expected, and it says so: a rule about converted funds has nothing to
report on a book containing none. The rest is genuinely untested, and it is listed as untested.

## Leaving a cell empty

The same rule applies in the reports. Where a figure cannot be computed honestly, the cell is empty and carries
its reason. A subtotal that would be
meaningless is omitted. A percentage that has lost its denominator does not
substitute one.

Somebody queries an empty cell. Nobody queries a number that looks
reasonable, which is how a wrong one ends up in an investor statement.

## What to ask any vendor

- ✓**Which figures are recomputed, and which are stored and read back?**
A figure computed once and read thereafter has nothing in the system able
to disagree with it.

- ✓**How often do the checks run, and across how many funds?**
At period end on a sample, or daily across all of them.

- ✓**Can you show me a check that did not run?**
If everything passes, ask how the system tells a pass from a check that
had nothing to examine.

- ✓**Where does a failure go?**
Ask whether it reaches a log or a worklist with an owner.

- [Which columns can be added, and which cannot](https://1494labs.com/notes/which-columns-can-be-added/), where the empty cell comes from

- [High-water marks and the partial redemption](https://1494labs.com/notes/high-water-marks-and-partial-redemptions/), one error of this kind, in numbers

- [What the platform does](https://1494labs.com/fund-accounting-software/)

- [Cash and reconciliation](https://docs.1494labs.com/guide/cash-and-reconciliation/) in the product docs: how cash is matched against the ledger

## How we handle it

The checks are part of how the platform is built.
A rule is written as a statement that must hold for every fund, and it
runs against every fund from then on: daily, and again after every
release. It reports what was never exercised alongside what failed. The
most recent run before this note was published covered every fund on the
platform and came back clean.

[Request a demo](https://1494labs.com/#contact)

Source: https://1494labs.com/notes/abor-and-ibor/

# ABOR and IBOR, and why most systems keep them apart

Two books, two clocks, and a reconciliation between them that nobody wants to
own. The split is a historical accident that hardened into an architecture, and
it is worth understanding before you buy a system that assumes it.

Fund accounting · roughly 6 minutes

## Accounting and Investment Books

The **accounting book of record** is the official set of books. It
is what the auditor examines, what the administrator calculates NAV from, and what
the financial statements are built on. It follows an accounting basis, respects
period boundaries, and is deliberately conservative about recognizing things
that have not happened yet.

The **investment book of record** is the position view the
investment team works from. It answers a different question: what do we own
right now, including the trade executed twenty minutes ago that will not settle
until Wednesday, and the corporate action that has been announced but not paid.

Both are correct. They disagree because they answer different questions on different clocks,
and that disagreement is expected. The trouble is what most firms have to
do about it.

## Why they diverge

Four sources of difference account for nearly all of it.

Where the two books part company

| Dimension | Accounting book | Investment book |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Clock** | Period-bounded, closed and locked | Continuous, intraday |
| **Recognition** | Trade date or settlement date, per policy, applied consistently | Everything known, including unsettled and pending |
| **Valuation** | Accounting basis, with a documented pricing hierarchy | Live or last marks, whatever is freshest |
| **Audience** | Auditors, administrators, LPs, regulators | Portfolio managers, risk, trading |

Say you buy a position on Monday, settling Wednesday, and the month ends
Tuesday.

The investment book shows the position on Monday, because you own the economic
exposure from the moment the trade is executed. The accounting book shows it on
Monday too if your policy is trade date, or on Wednesday if it is settlement
date, which means the position falls in the following month and the month-end
statements do not include it. Both answers are defensible under the right policy, because they answer
different questions.

## Why the split became architectural

The reason is historical, which is what makes it worth questioning.

Accounting systems were built for periodic close. They ran in batches, were designed around a monthly cycle, and optimized for producing a defensible
answer slowly. That was the right design when the alternative was paper.

Front offices needed something the accounting system could not give them: a
position view current as of this morning. So
a second system grew up beside the first, fed by the same trade files, keeping
its own version of the truth.

Once two systems hold overlapping data, a third thing appears whether anyone
designed it or not: **the reconciliation between them**. And
because that reconciliation is genuinely hard, an industry grew around it. Several
vendors now sell the reconciliation itself, which makes the split a source of
revenue for the people best placed to remove it.

The tell

If a platform sells you a reconciliation module between its own accounting
and its own position data, you are being sold a bridge between two
systems that arrived in one invoice.

## What the split actually costs

### A break list that never reaches zero

Every operations team that runs this architecture has a break list, and the
break list is never empty. Some breaks are real and matter. Most are timing
differences that will resolve themselves in two days. The expensive part is that
**a genuine problem sits in that list beside forty that will clear
themselves**, and people stop reading a list that has cried wolf for
six months.

### You cannot answer the obvious question

"What is our NAV right now?" is a reasonable question and, in a two-system
architecture, an unanswerable one. The accounting book knows as of the last
close. The investment book knows positions but not the accounting treatment.
Producing a current number means a person assembling it, which means it arrives
late and carries no assurance.

### Nobody can say which one is right

This is the corrosive one. When the two books disagree by a material amount and
the answer is needed today, someone has to adjudicate. That person is usually
the most senior operations person available, and their judgment is not
auditable. Over time the organization learns which book to trust for which
question, and that knowledge lives only in people's heads.

## The alternative, and what it actually requires

The alternative is to stop treating them as two books and start treating them
as **two views of one event stream**. Every economic event is
recorded once. Trade date and settlement date become two views of the same journal entries. The accounting view applies
period boundaries and recognition policy; the investment view does not. Neither
holds data the other lacks.

Under that design there is only one record, so there is no reconciliation
to automate. When a vendor says "our reconciliation is very good", it is
describing two books, and you should know which of the two designs you
are being shown.

It is also harder to build, for four reasons.

- **Every event must create its journal entry in one place.** The
moment any part of the system records a position without a journal entry, you have two books
again and you will not notice for a month.

- **The detail on each entry has to be rich enough for both audiences.**
Entity, fund, class, series, sleeve, currency, counterparty, custodian. If
the accounting model is thinner than the investment model, the investment
view has to be rebuilt somewhere else, and you are back where you started.

- **Close has to lock the period without stopping current work.** A
closed period must stay fixed for reporting while the current view keeps moving. Getting this
wrong in the safe direction gives you a system nobody can use intraday.

- **The agreement needs continuous proof.** If the two views are designed to agree, that agreement should still be
checked continuously, because designs fail quietly.

![A Statement of Changes in Partners' Capital, with beginning capital, contributions, allocations and ending capital.](https://1494labs.com/assets/screens/statement-of-changes.39e06e66.jpg)

**What one book looks like from the accounting side.**
This statement comes from the same journal entries the position and
exposure screens use, which is why its ending capital ties to the fund's
NAV to the cent. There is no extract between them to go stale.

## Four questions for a vendor

If you are evaluating platforms, these separate the architectures faster than a
feature matrix will.

1. **Where does the reconciliation between your accounting and position
data live?** If there is one, they are two systems. That may still be
the right purchase, but you should know what you are buying.

2. **When the two disagree, which one is authoritative, and who decides?**
A good answer names a rule. A bad answer names a person.

3. **Can you produce a NAV as of right now?**
Ask to see it done in the demo.

4. **What checks that the books are internally consistent, and how often
does it run?** "Our architecture guarantees it" is an assertion.
"These checks run every morning and here is today's output" is evidence.

A caveat worth stating

One ledger is not automatically the right answer for every firm. If your
accounting is genuinely simple and your investment process is genuinely
complex, or the reverse, two specialized systems and a small reconciliation
may cost less than migrating. The argument here is that the split should be a decision you made. Too
often it is an architecture inherited because that is how the software
was sold in 1998.

- [What an opening balance has to carry](https://1494labs.com/notes/what-an-opening-balance-has-to-carry/), if you are moving between the two architectures

- [Which columns can be added, and which cannot](https://1494labs.com/notes/which-columns-can-be-added/), once both books are one table

- [What one ledger looks like in practice](https://1494labs.com/fund-accounting-software/)

- [Securities and positions](https://docs.1494labs.com/guide/securities-and-positions/) in the product docs: lots, prices and corporate actions

## How we think about this

1494 Labs is built on the second model: the accounting book of record and the
investment book of record are views over one ledger, and the arithmetic is
re-checked every morning.

[Request a demo](https://1494labs.com/#contact)

Source: https://1494labs.com/notes/converting-from-a-fund-administrator/

# Converting from a fund administrator: prove the first close

Agree the handoff date, reconcile the opening records and reproduce the next fee calculation before accepting the new book.

Fund operations · November 3, 2026

## Agree what is changing hands

Start by naming the accounting record your team will maintain and the services the administrator will continue to provide. Set a cutover date with an approved NAV, ledger and investor statements. Assign an owner to each open reconciliation item and each source file. A data export is an input to the handoff; acceptance requires evidence that the new book works.

1. **Collect one consistent opening pack.** Take the trial balance, investment positions, cash reconciliations, investor capital and fee schedules at the same approved date. Preserve the original exports.

2. **Map the records.** Match ledger accounts, investment identifiers, investor accounts and currencies. Resolve duplicate or missing identifiers before loading balances.

3. **Carry the calculation state.** Include high-water marks, loss carryforwards, equalization balances, side-pocket participation and unused fee credits where applicable. For private equity, preserve dated cash flows needed by the agreed waterfall and performance calculations.

4. **Reconcile the opening book.** Match the ledger to NAV, positions to investment controls and every investor balance to the approved statements. Record each difference separately and keep unrelated breaks visible.

5. **Run a parallel period.** Use the same dated transactions, valuations and agreement terms. Compare fees and allocations before comparing final statements.

6. **Accept the evidence.** Have the controller approve the opening reconciliation, the parallel-period results and the process for correcting any remaining items.

## A fee-state acceptance test

Assume an investor opens with 5,000 shares at $80 and a high-water mark of $100 per share. Its opening value is $400,000 and its remaining loss below the mark is $100,000. A conversion can load the $400,000 balance correctly while losing that fee state.

As a test, recover the gross value to $100 per share with no intervening capital activity. Under an agreed high-water-mark-only fee, the recovery should generate no incentive fee. A fee charged on the $100,000 recovery signals that the imported balance and imported fee state need separate investigation.

## Keep the transition reviewable

Save the source pack, mapping, rejected records, approved adjustments and signed reconciliation together. Confirm who can correct the new book, how closed history remains available and how the team will handle a late administrator adjustment.

1494 Labs supports imports, configured fees and a traceable ledger. Bring a representative opening pack and the next-period acceptance tests to a [demo](https://1494labs.com/#contact), and agree the conversion scope before setting a live date.

Related: [what an opening balance has to carry](https://1494labs.com/notes/what-an-opening-balance-has-to-carry/) and [bringing data in](https://docs.1494labs.com/guide/bringing-data-in/).

Source: https://1494labs.com/notes/equalization-and-the-mid-period-subscriber/

# Equalization, and what a mid-period subscriber actually owes

An investor who subscribes after a drawdown can ride the recovery without
paying an incentive fee, because the loss being carried forward is somebody
else's. It is the normal consequence of running one
NAV per share, and there are only two ways out of it.

Hedge Funds · roughly 6 minutes

## The problem in one sentence

An incentive fee is charged on profit above a high-water mark. The mark
belongs to an investor, because it records what that investor has already
been charged on. A NAV per share belongs to the fund. Run a fund long
enough and those two facts collide: two investors holding identical shares
have different marks, and no single NAV per share can be correct for both.

## The free ride, with the numbers

A fund launches at $100 a share with a 20% incentive fee over a high-water
mark. Investor A subscribes $1,000,000 and receives 10,000 shares.

Year one is bad. The fund loses 20% and the NAV per share ends at $80. No
incentive fee is payable, correctly, because the fund is below its mark.
The mark stays at $100 and the fund carries forward a loss of $20 a share.

In January of year two, Investor B subscribes $800,000 at $80 and receives
10,000 shares. Year two is good: the manager returns 25% and the NAV per
share is back to $100.

End of year two, one NAV per share and one fund-level mark

| Investor | Subscribed | Now worth | Gain | Incentive fee paid |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A, in at $100 | $1,000,000 | $1,000,000 | $0 | $0 |
| B, in at $80 | $800,000 | $1,000,000 | $200,000 | $0 |

A is whole and owes nothing, which is right. B has made $200,000 and paid
nothing, which is not. The fund is exactly at its high-water mark, so at the
fund level no fee is due, and B's gain is sheltered by a loss B never
suffered. At 20% the manager has foregone **$40,000**, having
returned 25% to the investor who did not pay it.

Who pays

Nothing in the fund's accounts is out of balance here. The money was simply never charged. This is why the problem survives audits and
surfaces years later, usually when a manager finally reconstructs why a
strong year earned so little.

## The mirror case: a rebate nobody paid for

The same defect runs the other way when an investor buys into an accrual.

A fund sits at its mark of $100 in January and rises to $120 gross by June.
The administrator books a 20% accrual of $4 a share, so the published NAV
is $116. Investor B subscribes in July at $116. By December the fund has
given it all back: gross is $100, the accrual reverses in full, and the
published NAV is $100.

A is flat on the year and pays nothing, which is right. B paid $116 and
holds $100, a loss of $16 a share, on a gross move that was $20 a share. B
has absorbed $4 a share less than the market delivered, because B captured
the reversal of an accrual booked on gains earned between January and June,
when B was not in the fund. That $4 came out of A's pocket.

## Series accounting

Give each subscription date its own series of shares, with its own NAV and
its own high-water mark. In the first example B enters a second series at
$80, carrying a mark of $80. A's mark stays at $100.

End of year two, under series accounting

| Series | Own mark | NAV before fee | Gain above mark | Fee at 20% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1, Investor A | $100 | $100 | $0 | $0 |
| 2, Investor B | $80 | $100 | $200,000 | $40,000 |

Both answers are now right, and neither investor subsidizes the other. The
cost is that the fund is no longer one book. A fund open for monthly
subscriptions creates twelve series in its first year, each needing its own
NAV, its own mark and its own fee calculation every period.

That count is usually managed by consolidating series into a lead series at
year end, once a series has crystallized and stands at its own mark. Series
still below their mark cannot be consolidated: they carry a loss
carryforward the lead series does not, and merging them would hand that
shelter to everyone. So the series that persist are precisely the ones
nobody wants to explain, and two investors a month apart will see different
NAVs per share for what they were sold as the same fund.

## Equalization, on a single NAV

The alternative keeps one NAV per share and corrects each investor
individually at subscription. Two situations, two corrections, running in
opposite directions.

What the correction has to undo

| Investor subscribes | Without a correction | The correction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Below the fund's mark, while a loss is carried forward | Rides the recovery without paying, sheltered by someone else's loss | Charged on each investor's gain as the fund recovers, typically by redeeming shares from them |
| Above the mark mid-period, into an accrual already in the NAV | Captures a rebate if the accrual reverses, on a fee they never bore | Pays an additional amount alongside the subscription, returned to them to the extent the accrual reverses |

One NAV per share survives, and every investor pays on that investor's profit
measured from their own entry. What it costs is that an investor's economics
no longer live entirely in their share count. A per-investor adjustment
account has to be carried, applied on the right events and shown on a
statement, and it moves for reasons the NAV per share does not explain.

Terminology

These mechanisms travel under names that are not used consistently:
equalization credit, depreciation deposit, contingent redemption,
equalization factor. Two administrators will use the same word for
different mechanics, and the offering document will sometimes use a third.
When comparing two funds, compare the mechanism and run the same example
through each. The label tells you very little.

## The problem comes from issuing shares

Everything above is a consequence of issuing units. A fund that allocates profit to capital accounts never meets it. Each partner has an
account, each account carries its own high-water mark, and profit is allocated to each account directly. Two partners who joined two years apart have two different marks and
nothing has to reconcile them, because there is no single per-unit number
trying to be correct for both.

That is why a US onshore limited partnership generally has no equalization
mechanism at all, and why the topic is barely mentioned in partnership
accounting. The offshore company issuing shares has the opposite
constraint: it needs one dealing NAV per share, quoted to investors and used
for subscriptions and redemptions, and that single number is exactly what
cannot be right for everybody.

The awkward case is the structure that has both. A master-feeder with an
onshore partnership feeder and an offshore corporate feeder runs
capital-account mechanics on one side and share mechanics on the other,
against the same underlying book. The two feeders are not doing the same
arithmetic, they should not produce the same per-investor answer, and a
system that models only one of the two will quietly force the other into its
shape.

## What to check

- ✓**Is the high-water mark held per investor or per fund?**
One mark for the whole fund is the tell. It cannot be simultaneously
correct for two investors who entered at different levels, and no amount
of reporting on top will fix it.

- ✓**What happens on a partial redemption?**
A mark that is not reduced when half the money leaves shelters the
remainder against a loss it no longer carries. This has its own
arithmetic, covered in the note below.

- ✓**Does the statement show the adjustment?**
An equalization amount buried inside a NAV per share is an amount the
investor cannot check, and it is the line they will eventually ask about.

- ✓**What happens to the series count at year end?**
Ask which series consolidate, which cannot, and what the count looks like
in year three.

- [High-water marks and the partial redemption](https://1494labs.com/notes/high-water-marks-and-partial-redemptions/), the same mark on the way out

- [Hedge fund accounting](https://1494labs.com/hedge-fund-accounting/), including series and crystallization

- [The investor lifecycle](https://docs.1494labs.com/guide/the-investor-lifecycle/) in the product docs: subscriptions, redemptions and transfers as ledger events

## How we handle it

1494 Labs carries the high-water mark per series and per capital account, and supports both models: series accounting with a separate series for each subscription period, and equalization on a single NAV. Which one a
fund uses is a setting on the fund, because the answer is in its offering document.

[Request a demo](https://1494labs.com/#contact)

# Equalization at conversion: check each subscriber separately

Two investors can hold the same number of shares and need different fee outcomes. Test the imported records investor by investor.

Fund operations · November 3, 2026

## Preserve the method as well as the balance

Record whether the fund uses series accounting or a single NAV with investor-level equalization adjustments. Preserve the relevant subscription dates, quantities, fee rates, marks, outstanding credits or deficits, and settlement history. Confirm whether each reported balance is before or after accrued fees and equalization adjustments.

Do not translate a credit into a high-water mark, or merge series, merely because two opening NAV totals agree. The governing terms determine the method and the records needed to continue it.

1. Agree the method and crystallization dates with the controller and the outgoing provider.

2. Reconcile each investor's quantity, opening value and fee-state record to the source schedule.

3. Identify subscribers who entered above the existing mark, below it and at it.

4. Run recovery, further-gain and reversal cases under the same agreed assumptions in both books.

5. Compare each investor's fee and closing economics, then reconcile the total to the ledger.

6. Test a redemption and any pending equalization settlement before accepting the setup.

## A recovery case that separates the investors

Assume a 20% incentive fee on gains above each investor's own mark, no hurdle, no other fees and no intervening capital activity. A subscribed at $100; B subscribed after a decline at $80. Each holds 10,000 shares. The test ends at a gross, pre-incentive-fee value of $100 per share.

| Investor | Own mark | Gross test value | Gain above own mark | Expected fee |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | $100 | $1,000,000 | $0 | $0 |
| B | $80 | $1,000,000 | $200,000 | $40,000 |

Separate series can carry those marks directly. A single-NAV method needs the appropriate investor adjustments to reach the agreed economics. Compare the resulting investor values and fee allocations; do not require identical journal lines from methods with different mechanics.

## Investigate a total that ties

A fund-level reconciliation does not prove that the fee was charged to the correct investors. Trace any difference through the subscription price, imported fee state, adjustment postings and settlement. Retain the original state and the expected test result alongside the conversion evidence.

[The mid-period subscriber example](https://1494labs.com/notes/equalization-and-the-mid-period-subscriber/) explains the underlying problem. Ask to see both supported approaches in a [1494 Labs demonstration](https://1494labs.com/#contact).

Source: https://1494labs.com/notes/european-vs-american-waterfall/

# American vs European waterfall on the same two deals

The difference is usually explained as "whole-of-fund versus deal-by-deal" and
then left there. Run the same two deals through both and the consequence shows
up as a specific number: six million dollars sitting in the wrong pocket.

Private equity · roughly 6 minutes

## The mechanism, briefly

Both structures distribute money through the same four tiers, in the same
order. What differs is *what the tiers are measured against*.

1. **Return of capital.** Investors get their contributions back.

2. **Preferred return.** Investors receive a hurdle, commonly 8%, before the manager participates in profit.

3. **Catch-up.** The manager receives most or all of the next dollars until it holds its full percentage of profit, typically 20%.

4. **Split.** Everything after that divides at the carry rate, commonly 80/20.

In a **European** waterfall, those tiers are measured across the
entire fund. No carry is paid until investors have received back
*all* contributed capital and their preferred return on it.

In an **American** waterfall, the tiers are measured deal by deal.
A profitable exit can pay carry while other investments are still outstanding,
and while the fund as a whole has returned nothing.

## The same fund, both ways

Take a fund of $100M in commitments, 20% carry over an 8% preferred return. It
makes two investments and incurs $20M of fees and expenses across its life.

The fund

| Item | Amount | Timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deal A invested | $40M | Year 1 |
| Deal B invested | $40M | Year 1 |
| Fees and expenses | $20M | Across the life |
| Total contributed | $100M | |
| Deal A exits | $100M | Year 3 |
| Deal B exits | $20M | Year 5 |
| Total proceeds | $120M | |

Across the whole fund the arithmetic is simple. Investors put in $100M and
$120M comes back. **Total profit is $20M, so carry at 20% should be
$4M.** That figure is not in dispute under either structure. What
differs is when the manager gets paid, and what happens in between.

Simplification

The preferred return below is shown as a simple, non-compounding figure to
keep the mechanism visible. Real agreements specify compounding, the base it
accrues on, and whether it is charged on fees as well as investments. Those choices move the numbers; the shape of the result stays the same.

## American: the manager is paid in year 3

Deal A exits for $100M on $40M invested. Under a deal-by-deal waterfall, the
tiers run against *that deal*.

Year 3, Deal A proceeds of $100M

| Tier | To investors | To manager |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Return of Deal A capital | $40M | $0 |
| Preferred return on that capital | $10M | $0 |
| Remaining $50M, split 80/20 | $40M | $10M |
| Distributed | $90M | $10M |

The manager has now received **$10M of carry**, and on the evidence
available in year 3 that looks entirely earned. Deal A was excellent.

Then Deal B exits in year 5 for $20M against $40M invested. All $20M goes to
investors; there is no profit to share. The fund is over.

Final position, American waterfall

| Party | Contributed | Received | Net |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Investors | $100M | $110M | $10M |
| Manager | $0 | $10M | $10M |

The manager took **half** of the fund's $20M profit, on a deal
structured to pay 20%. Investors are owed $6M back.

## European: the manager is paid in year 5

Same deals, same order, tiers measured across the fund.

Deal A exits for $100M in year 3. Investors have contributed $100M, so the
entire distribution returns capital. Capital is now repaid in full, but the
preferred return has not been satisfied and no profit has been recognized.
**The manager receives nothing.**

Deal B exits for $20M in year 5. Capital is already back, so this is the first
money available for the later tiers.

Year 5, remaining $20M

| Tier | To investors | To manager |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Preferred return | $16M | $0 |
| Catch-up to 20% of the $20M profit | $0 | $4M |
| Distributed | $16M | $4M |

Final position, European waterfall

| Party | Contributed | Received | Net |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Investors | $100M | $116M | $16M |
| Manager | $0 | $4M | $4M |

$4M of carry on $20M of profit. Exactly 20%, arrived at without anyone
needing to give money back.

## The difference in one line

Same deals, same total proceeds

| | American | European |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carry paid | $10M | $4M |
| Carry earned | $4M | $4M |
| Owed back | $6M | $0 |
| First payment | Year 3 | Year 5 |

The manager *earned* $4M under both. The American waterfall moved
**when it was paid**, and created a $6M
obligation that has to be honored years later.

## Which brings us to clawback

Every American waterfall carries a clawback provision requiring the manager to
return excess carry at the end of the fund. On paper this makes the two
structures equivalent. In practice it is the weakest part of the arrangement,
for reasons that have nothing to do with anyone's good faith.

- **The money was taxed on receipt.** Carry distributed in year 3
was income in year 3. Returning the gross amount in year 5 means the manager
repays money it never fully kept, unless the agreement provides for after-tax
clawback, which shifts the shortfall to investors.

- **Carry is distributed to individuals.** By year 5 some of those
people have left, retired, divorced, or died. The obligation may sit with the
management entity while the money sits with individuals, and collecting it is a governance problem.

- **It arrives at the worst moment.** A clawback is triggered by
the fund underperforming, which is the same condition under which the manager
is least able to pay.

The standard mitigations are worth knowing because they are negotiable.
**Escrow** holds back a percentage of each carry distribution,
often 20% to 30%, until the fund is wound up. **Interim clawback
tests** run the whole-fund calculation periodically through the fund's life, so an
overpayment surfaces in year 4, four years before the final test would find it.
**Guarantees** from individual principals make the obligation personal to the principals.

The accounting consequence

An American waterfall means every carry figure in your books is provisional
until the fund closes. A system that records carry as settled fact will report numbers it cannot
defend later. Carry belongs on the books as an accrual subject to a
whole-fund test, and interim clawback testing belongs in the ledger with it.

## Most funds are neither, exactly

The two-way split is a teaching device. Real agreements sit on a spectrum, and
the interesting terms are the ones that move a fund along it.

- **Deal-by-deal with a loss carryforward.** American in timing,
but realized losses on other investments must be recovered before carry is
paid. Removes much of the exposure in our example.

- **Deal-by-deal with return of all invested capital first.** Carry waits until every dollar deployed to date has come back, from every
deal including the ones still held.

- **Whole-of-fund with an early carry release.** European by
default, but permitting carry once coverage tests are met, such as remaining
holdings being valued at some multiple of unreturned capital.

- **Catch-up rates that are not 100%.** A 50% or 80% catch-up
changes the split materially and is easy to miss when reading quickly.

## What to check in the agreement

If you are modeling a fund and want to know which structure you actually have,
these determine it:

1. Are the tiers measured against the fund or against each investment?

2. Does the preferred return compound, and on what base? Does it accrue on fees as well as capital?

3. Is there a loss carryforward, and does it cover unrealized write-downs or only realized losses?

4. What is the catch-up rate, and is it 100%?

5. Is there an escrow, at what percentage, and when does it release?

6. Is clawback gross or after-tax, and is it guaranteed by individuals?

7. How often is the interim clawback test run?

Those seven answers reconstruct the waterfall. Everything else is detail
around them.

![A waterfall policy with four tiers - return of capital, accrued preferred, GP catch-up to 20 percent at 100 percent, split 80/20 - a clawback measurement per LP showing no exposure, and a posted distribution of $12,075,209.34: $9,300,000.00 returned as capital and $153,070.79 of GP carry.](https://1494labs.com/assets/screens/distribution-waterfall.446c8f15.jpg)
**The same seven answers, entered as tiers.** The split below is computed from them, and the GP's clawback exposure is measured beside the policy, per LP by default, so an interim test reads straight off the screen.

- [What an opening balance has to carry](https://1494labs.com/notes/what-an-opening-balance-has-to-carry/), including where a converted fund sits in its own waterfall

- [Private equity fund accounting](https://1494labs.com/private-equity-fund-accounting/), with the waterfall computed on the book

- [Capital calls and distributions](https://docs.1494labs.com/guide/capital-calls-and-distributions/) in the product docs: what happens when carry has to come back

- [GP economics](https://docs.1494labs.com/guide/gp-economics/) in the product docs: how carry is split among principals and how it vests

## How we think about this

1494 Labs models waterfalls as configurable tiers,
because the agreements we read are rarely either textbook case. Carry is held as an accrual subject to a whole-fund test.

[Request a demo](https://1494labs.com/#contact)

# High-water-mark acceptance tests before the first live close

Use a recovery, a partial redemption and a gain above the mark to check that the fee engine retained the right investor state.

Fund operations · November 3, 2026

## Write down the expected economics first

Fix the fee terms, share quantity, gross value convention, high-water mark, crystallization dates and rounding rules before testing. The examples below assume a 20% incentive fee above the investor's existing high-water mark, no hurdle, no other fees and no cash flows except the stated redemption.

1. **Record the opening state.** Keep the per-share mark and the quantity it belongs to, alongside any total loss carried forward.

2. **Recover to the mark.** Confirm that a recovery through an existing loss does not create a fee under these terms.

3. **Redeem part of the holding below the mark.** Check that the state left behind belongs to the remaining shares.

4. **Recover beyond the mark.** Independently calculate the gain above the mark and the resulting fee.

5. **Check the posting and investor statement.** Trace the fee from its calculation through the ledger to the investor's ending value.

## Three checkpoints on the same holding

The investor starts with 10,000 shares at $80 and a $100 per-share mark. The opening shortfall is $200,000. It redeems 5,000 shares at $80, leaving 5,000 shares and a $100,000 shortfall.

| Checkpoint | Remaining shares | Gross price | Gain above $100 mark | Fee at 20% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| After partial redemption | 5,000 | $80 | $0 | $0 |
| Recovery to mark | 5,000 | $100 | $0 | $0 |
| Recovery beyond mark | 5,000 | $120 | $100,000 | $20,000 |

The final checkpoint follows directly from 5,000 × ($120 − $100) × 20%. Keeping the original $200,000 total shortfall after half the shares leave would shelter too much of the recovery. The per-share mark stays $100 in this example; the total state changes with the quantity.

## Extend the test to the actual fund terms

Add separate cases for new subscriptions, transfers, full redemptions, fee accrual reversals and the fund's own crystallization rules. Record expected results before running the system. Check the imported opening state again whenever a correct total conceals an unexpected investor fee.

1494 Labs supports investor fee calculations and a traceable ledger. Use these cases to make a [demonstration](https://1494labs.com/#contact) specific. [High-water marks and partial redemptions](https://1494labs.com/notes/high-water-marks-and-partial-redemptions/) explains the mechanism behind the test.


---

Source: https://1494labs.com/notes/high-water-marks-and-partial-redemptions/

# High-water marks and the partial redemption

A high-water mark is easy to get right while nothing moves. The mistakes
happen on the way out: a partial redemption that leaves a stale loss
carryforward behind, and a full redemption that walks past an accrued fee.
Neither one breaks anything that would tell you.

Fees · roughly 4 minutes

## The mark is a level, and it belongs to the holder

A high-water mark records the highest value on which an investor has
already been charged an incentive fee. Above it, profit is new and
chargeable. Below it, the shortfall is a loss carried forward, and the
manager works back through it for nothing.

The mark therefore belongs to a holder, and it is attached
to a quantity of shares. That second half is the part that gets lost: change
the quantity and the mark has to change with it.

## What a partial redemption has to do

An investor holds 10,000 shares. The mark is $100 a share and the NAV has
fallen to $80, so $200,000 of loss is carried forward. The investor redeems
5,000 shares at $80, taking out $400,000, and leaves 5,000 shares behind.

The fund then recovers to $120 a share. Here is the same position under two
treatments of that carryforward.

5,000 remaining shares, $80 to $120

| | Carryforward left | Gain on the remainder | Chargeable | Fee at 20% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Carryforward left untouched | $200,000 | $200,000 | $0 | $0 |
| Carryforward released pro rata | $100,000 | $200,000 | $100,000 | $20,000 |

The second line is the right one, and it is easy to prove without reference
to any carryforward at all. The remaining 5,000 shares went from a mark of
$100 to a NAV of $120. That is $20 a share of genuinely new profit, $100,000,
and 20% of it is $20,000.

The first line shelters that profit behind a loss the investor took half of
out of the fund in cash. Redeeming released half the shares, and the loss
attached to them left with them.

Why it survives

Nothing fails in the first line. The trial balance foots, the capital
accounts tie, the NAV is right, and the investor's statement is correct in
every figure it shows. The fee is simply smaller than it should be, and
there is no number anywhere that it disagrees with.

Note also the direction. The error never runs the other way. Skipping the
proration always shelters profit, which always favors the investor and
always costs the manager. An error with a consistent sign accumulates period after period, and it recurs every time an investor trims a position
during a drawdown.

## The other direction: redeeming above the mark

The same investor, but the fund is at $120 against a mark of $100 and an
incentive fee is accruing. On 10,000 shares the accrual attributable to them
is 20% of $20 a share, or $40,000.

They redeem in full at $120. If the fee is only settled at period end, they
leave with $1,200,000 and the accrual they generated reverses across the
investors who stayed. The fee has to **crystallize at the redemption
date**: $40,000 is charged then, and the investor receives $1,160,000.

On a partial redemption the same thing happens proportionally. Redeem 40% and
40% of the accrual crystallizes, $16,000, while the remaining 60% keeps its
mark of $100 and carries on accruing.

The ordering matters

Crystallize before setting the redemption price. A fee
calculated on a NAV that has already had the redemption taken out of it is
a fee on the wrong base, and the difference is not rounding.

## Transfers are not redemptions

When shares move between two investors, nothing has been realized and no
money has left the fund. The mark travels with the shares: the receiving
holder inherits it at the level the transferring holder carried, along with
any loss carried forward against them.

Treating a transfer as a redemption and a subscription resets the mark to the
current NAV. If the shares were underwater that quietly cancels a loss
carryforward the manager was still working through, and hands the incoming
holder a fee-free ride on the recovery.

## What to check

- ✓**Is the mark stored as a level or as an amount?**
A level per share prorates automatically when the share count changes. An
amount has to be adjusted explicitly on every partial redemption, and that
adjustment is what gets forgotten.

- ✓**Does a redemption crystallize, or wait for period end?**
Waiting means a departing investor's fee is paid by the investors who
stayed.

- ✓**Does a transfer carry the mark?**
Ask what happens to a loss carryforward when shares change hands.

- ✓**Can you produce the mark's history for one investor?**
Set at subscription, reduced by each partial redemption, reset by each
crystallization. If that history cannot be reconstructed, the current
number cannot be checked by anyone, including an auditor.

- [Equalization, and what a mid-period subscriber actually owes](https://1494labs.com/notes/equalization-and-the-mid-period-subscriber/), the same mark on the way in

- [Hedge fund accounting](https://1494labs.com/hedge-fund-accounting/), including crystallization and loss carryforwards

- [Fees: from structure to charge](https://docs.1494labs.com/guide/fees-from-structure-to-charge/) in the product docs, from accrual to crystallization

## How we handle it

1494 Labs holds the mark per capital account as a level, prorates it on
partial redemption, and crystallizes on the redemption date. Every change to a mark is an event with a source, so the
history can be read back for any investor on any date.

# Management fee offsets: reconcile the fee before and after the credit

A fee offset is a calculation with a source, a percentage and a period. Keep all three visible, along with any amount carried forward.

Fund operations · November 3, 2026

## Read the offset terms before calculating

Some fund agreements reduce the management fee by specified portfolio-company fees. The offset percentage, eligible fee types, timing and treatment of unused amounts come from the governing agreement and disclosures. Do not assume every receipt qualifies or every investor has the same arrangement.

1. Calculate the gross management fee from the agreed base, rate and period.

2. List eligible receipts with their dates, source companies and supporting records.

3. Apply the contractual offset percentage and any allocation across funds.

4. Apply the available credit to the fee, respecting any cap.

5. Reconcile the net fee and any unused credit to the ledger and the next period's opening record.

## A worked quarter

Assume the gross quarterly management fee is $250,000, eligible receipts are $80,000 and the agreement provides a 100% offset in that quarter. There are no opening credits or other adjustments.

| Calculation | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Gross management fee | $250,000 |
| Eligible receipts × 100% | $80,000 |
| Net management fee | $170,000 |

If eligible credits were $300,000 instead, a fee capped at zero would consume $250,000. The remaining $50,000 carries forward only if the terms allow it. A negative payable should not appear simply because the spreadsheet subtracts one cell from another.

## Check the receipt trail as well as the arithmetic

The SEC's June 2020 examination risk alert describes failures to apply offsets in accordance with disclosures and failures to track portfolio-company fees. That is a reason to reconcile the eligible-receipt register as well as the net invoice.

Review credits received by affiliates, timing differences and investor-specific terms against the agreement. Keep the gross fee, applied credit and closing credit balance separately visible so a reviewer can reproduce the result.

In a software evaluation, bring one ordinary quarter and one quarter where credits exceed the fee. Ask the provider to show the source receipts, the applied amount and the next quarter's opening credit.

Source: [SEC examination risk alert, June 23, 2020, fees and expenses](https://www.sec.gov/files/Private%20Fund%20Risk%20Alert_0.pdf). The numerical example illustrates assumed contract terms.


---

Source: https://1494labs.com/notes/moving-a-fund-off-spreadsheets/

# Moving a fund off spreadsheets: prove the opening book first

Choose a cutover date, carry the calculation state and run a parallel close. A trial balance alone is not a complete fund conversion.

Fund operations · November 3, 2026

## Choose one cutover period

Start with a period whose ledger, NAV and investor statements have been reconciled. Save those reports and the source workbooks as the conversion evidence. Decide which historical records must remain queryable and which calculations must continue from the opening position.

1. Map ledger accounts, investments and investor accounts to the new system.

2. Import the opening trial balance and reconcile debits, credits and NAV.

3. Reconcile investment quantities, cost and value, then each investor's capital.

4. Carry the state behind the next calculation: high-water marks, loss carryforwards, fee credits and side-pocket interests where applicable.

5. For private equity, preserve dated contributions and distributions needed for performance and waterfall calculations.

6. Run the next period in parallel and investigate differences before accepting the conversion.

## A conversion that ties but still fails

Suppose an investor opens at $900,000 with a $1 million high-water mark. Importing only the $900,000 balance can make the opening ledger and investor statement agree. It does not tell the fee engine that the next $100,000 of recovery is below the existing mark.

The acceptance test is the next calculation as well as the opening balance. Run a recovery period and compare the fee with the old workbook under the same terms. Keep any differences visible until the controller can explain them.

## Agree the acceptance evidence

- Opening ledger balances and NAV reconcile to the approved source.

- Investment and investor subledgers agree with their ledger controls.

- Fees, allocations and distributions reproduce the agreed examples.

- Historical statements remain available, with the cutover boundary clear.

- A reviewer can trace a reported number back to its imported record or new-period entry.

A workbook can remain useful for independent checks. Give the accounting system responsibility for the accepted book, and document who approves corrections during the parallel period.

Ask 1494 Labs to demonstrate imports and a close using reference data shaped like your fund. Agree the scope of any mid-life conversion before scheduling it.

[What an opening balance has to carry](https://1494labs.com/notes/what-an-opening-balance-has-to-carry/) covers the calculation state in more detail. [See the platform](https://1494labs.com/fund-accounting-software/) or [request a demo](https://1494labs.com/#contact).


---

Source: https://1494labs.com/notes/side-pockets-and-investor-participation/

# Side pockets: keep the investment and its investors together

A side pocket needs its own participation record. A later subscriber should not silently acquire an interest in an earlier illiquid investment.

Fund operations · November 3, 2026

## Start with who participates

A side pocket separates an investment from the main pool for accounting and investor participation. The fund documents determine who participates, how it is valued and when proceeds can be distributed. A separate security label alone does not preserve those terms.

1. Identify the investment and the effective date of the side pocket.

2. Record the participating investors and their interests on that date.

3. Keep subsequent subscriptions and redemptions in the main pool from changing that participation unless the governing terms require it.

4. Allocate the side pocket's valuation changes, income and expenses to its participants.

5. At realization, reconcile proceeds and remaining balances to those same investors.

## A small example

Assume an investment worth $1 million is placed in a side pocket when investor A owns 60% and investor B owns 40% of the participating capital. Investor C subscribes to the main pool later. Under terms that fix side-pocket participation at designation, C has no interest in this investment.

| Investor | Opening side-pocket interest | Share of a $100,000 gain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | $600,000 | $60,000 |
| B | $400,000 | $40,000 |
| C | $0 | $0 |
| Total | $1,000,000 | $100,000 |

The example excludes fees and cash flows. Those need their own treatment under the fund's terms; they should not be inferred from the gain allocation.

## What the controller checks

Reconcile the investment's carrying value to the sum of its investor interests. Then check the participation record independently. A total that ties can still allocate money to the wrong investors. Test a subscription after designation, a partial redemption and a realization before relying on the setup.

During conversion, carry the side-pocket participation record with the opening values. Rebuilding interests from today's main-pool percentages can change the economics while leaving total NAV unchanged.

1494 Labs supports hedge funds with side pockets. Ask to see the investor participation and the allocation trail in a demonstration of your fund's terms.

[What an opening balance has to carry](https://1494labs.com/notes/what-an-opening-balance-has-to-carry/) explains the other records a conversion needs.


---

Source: https://1494labs.com/notes/what-an-opening-balance-has-to-carry/

# What an opening balance has to carry

A trial balance tells you where a fund stands. It does not tell you enough to
compute what happens next, because the calculations that matter carry history forward, and the history
they need is not on any document you can request from a custodian.

Conversion · roughly 5 minutes

## Standing still versus carrying on

A conversion is usually scoped as loading balances: cash, positions,
receivables, payables, capital. That work is real, and it is the easy part. Balances describe a fund at rest. The question a new system has to
answer on its first working day is the other one, which is what happens
next, and several of the calculations that answer it depend on things that
already happened.

## What the next calculation needs

State required to compute the first post-conversion period

| The next thing you compute | What it needs from before the cut | In a trial balance? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Incentive fee | High-water mark and loss carryforward, per investor or series | No |
| Incentive fee for a mid-period subscriber | That investor's equalization position | No |
| Realized gain on the next sale | Cost basis by lot, and the cost-flow convention that picks between them | No |
| An investor's capital account | Per-investor contributions, distributions and allocated profit to date | The fund total only |
| Where the next distribution falls | Distributed to date and carry paid to date, cumulatively | No |
| Uncalled commitment | Called, plus whatever has been distributed subject to recall | No |
| The performance record | The return series and the dates it was calculated on | No |

## Fee history is the part that gets left behind

Positions and cash are physical. Somebody can pull a custody statement and
check them, and if they are wrong it shows up immediately and loudly.

Fee history is different in kind. A high-water mark is a memory of
something that already happened. There is no counterparty holding a copy, no
statement to reconcile against, and no external document that records it. It
exists inside the system being switched off.

That makes it the most likely thing to be dropped and the least likely to be
noticed. A fund converted without its marks reconciles perfectly on day one
and stays perfect until the first incentive calculation, which will be wrong
by an amount nobody can reconstruct, because the evidence needed to
reconstruct it was in the system that has since been decommissioned.

Ask early

Whether the outgoing system can export marks, loss carryforwards and
equalization positions per investor is worth establishing before a migration date is agreed. If the answer is no, that is a
constraint on the whole project, and it is cheaper to discover in a
meeting than in a fee run.

## Closed-end funds: the waterfall is path-dependent

For a drawdown fund the tiers are measured cumulatively across the life of
the fund. What the next distribution pays depends entirely on what has
already been paid: whether capital is back, whether the preferred return has
been satisfied, whether the manager is still in catch-up.

A fund converted with a balance sheet and a commitment schedule has no
position in that sequence at all. It cannot say which tier the next dollar
belongs to, and the first distribution after the cut will be computed from
the beginning of a waterfall that is already years in.

Uncalled commitment has the same shape. It is commitment minus called, plus any distributions made subject to
recall, and whether a given distribution was recallable is a term in the
agreement that the cash movement does not carry.

## Two different things called history

Prior periods can come across in one of two ways, and they are routinely
conflated in the same sentence.

| | Reporting-only | Rebuilt |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What arrives | The results: balances, statements, capital accounts as reported | The underlying activity, transaction by transaction |
| What you can do | Display it, print it, answer "show me last year" | Re-run an allocation, restate a period, change an assumption |
| What it needs | The old system's output | The old system's inputs, in usable form |
| Typical cost | Part of the conversion | A project of its own, and often not possible |

Reporting-only is an honest and usually correct answer. The failure is
buying it while expecting the other one, and then discovering the difference
during an audit. Pre-conversion periods should be marked as what they are,
so that a reporting-only period cannot be mistaken for one that would recompute if
you asked it to.

## The test that settles it

Before the old system is switched off, run the first post-conversion period
on both and compare. Three specific comparisons are worth more than a
reconciliation of totals:

- ✓**The incentive fee, per investor.**
A fund total can be right while two investors are
wrong in opposite directions, and that is exactly what a missing mark
looks like.

- ✓**One realized sale.**
This tests that lots and the cost-flow convention came across along with the position's market value.

- ✓**One distribution, on a closed-end fund.**
This tests that the fund knows where it stands in its own waterfall.

If that comparison cannot be run because the old system is already gone, the fund was only re-keyed, and the first calculation that
depends on history will be the one that finds out.

## What to ask a vendor

- ✓**Is there a conversion date built into the fund record**,
or does every fund have to start at inception?

- ✓**Where does a high-water mark go in?**
If there is no field for it, it is being reverse-engineered from a
transaction history you do not have.

- ✓**Are pre-conversion periods marked**,
or do they present exactly like periods the system computed itself?

- ✓**What happens when an error is found in a pre-conversion period?**
There is a right answer, which is that it is corrected as a restatement
with the original preserved, and a wrong one, which is that somebody edits the reported figures.

- [High-water marks and the partial redemption](https://1494labs.com/notes/high-water-marks-and-partial-redemptions/), the state most likely to be missing

- [What the platform does](https://1494labs.com/fund-accounting-software/), including conversion-mode onboarding

- [Bringing data in](https://docs.1494labs.com/guide/bringing-data-in/) in the product docs: carrying high-water marks through a conversion

## How we handle it

1494 Labs models a conversion date on the fund. Periods before it are locked from the start and marked pre-conversion, so a
reporting-only period can never be mistaken for a computed one, and the
opening position carries fee history alongside the balances. Converting an existing book is quoted separately from
the subscription, and it is free for the first five early adopters.
